newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FOCUS - Bulgarian lev hits new lows against dollar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bulgarian lev hits new lows against dollar.

text.p: The Bulgarian lev fell to new lows against the dollar in cautious trade on the interbank market on Wednesday and dealers said they expected further falls ahead of introduction of tough new monetary measures.
The lev fell to 397.5 to the dollar in early trade from Tuesday's 386.5 close and dealers reported trade at 414 levs towards noon.
The currency collapsed dramatically two weeks ago as Bulgarians rushed to convert their savings to dollars, losing 30 percent of its value in a week and touching a low of 395.

A "gentlemen's agreement" between the central bank and commercial banks to halt speculation helped the lev recover some of its losses, but with the central bank holding back from intervention to save its dwindling reserves, the currency has drifted lower again this week.

"The trend will be for further lev depreciation, and the rate of depreciation depends on foreign currency demand from large clients and certainly on the central bank's willingness to support the lev," one dealer said.
A series of bank collapses has eroded confidence among Bulgaria's financial institutions, making the interbank market very thin and easy to manipulate.
"The domestic forex market is experiencing low dollar liquidity in which even relatively small demand may strongly pressure the lev," said one dealer.
At the suggestion of the International Monetary Fund, the government and the central bank have agreed to set up a currency board early next year to stabilise the economy and halt the lev's slide.

A currency board is a form of fixed exchange rate regime which requires that levs in circulation and commercial banks' mimimum reserves at the central bank match central bank foreign exchange and gold reserves.
Economists say the exchange rate at which the board is introduced needs to be depreciated enough to give sufficient cover but appreciated enough not to lock in a high inflation rate.

International Monetary Fund Resident Representative Franek Rozwadowski said on Friday central bank foreign exchange and gold reserves were sufficient to set up a currency board at the current exchange rate or even a more appreciated one. The lev closed on Friday at 363.

Central bank reserves were $541 million at the end of October. The bank has gold reserves worth about $400 million and levs in circulation and commercial banks' minumum reserve deposits at the central bank total 180 billion levs.
However, it is not yet clear how Bulgaria will support a currency board and also meet debt payments of $300 million which fall due in the first quarter of 1997.

The government has asked for extra cash from the IMF and other lenders. The IMF may rebundle its existing $580 million standby accord, from which it has disbursed $115 million, but diplomats say there are no immediate plans for other funding.
Bulgaria lacks foreign investment which would bring in hard currency, and declining domestic production means lower export income.

The government is negotiating the sale of a 60 percent stake in its Sodi Devnya soda ash plant to U.S. firm General Chemical Group Inc. Deputy Prime Minister Roumen Gechev said last month the sale would raise $160 million and the company had pledged investments of $118 million over five years.
